A package is like a book: __init__.py is the table of contents. The actual chapters (submodules) can be organized however you like internally. The table of contents decides what readers see — they don't need to know which chapter a topic lives in, just that it's in the book.

A virtual environment is a private sandbox for your project's Python installation. Packages you install inside it stay inside it — they don't leak into other projects, and other projects' packages don't leak in. Each project gets its own clean room.

cards.teaser: `requirements.txt` is the conventional filename for a list of pip-installable dependencies, one per line. `pip install -r requirements.txt` reproduces the dependency set exactly — the foundation of reproducible Python environments.

cards.title: Absolute vs Relative Imports

Absolute imports are like writing a full mailing address — unambiguous no matter where you read the letter. Relative imports are like saying 'the building next door' — clear in context but confusing if you don't know where you're standing. cards.title: Lock Files (pip-tools, poetry)
cards.teaser: A lock file records the exact resolved version of every dependency — direct and transitive — that was tested and known to work. Reproducing the same environment on any machine is impossible without one.

runs.text: states what you want; a lock file states exactly what you got.
(your direct dependencies with loose pins) and resolves the full dependency graph, writing a fully pinned
with every transitive package, its version, and its hash.
resolves and locks in one step.
reproduces the exact locked environment. Both tools integrate hash checking — pip refuses to install a package whose hash doesn't match the lock file, preventing supply chain attacks.

items.text: (Astral, 2024) is a Rust-based replacement for pip + pip-tools that resolves and installs 10–100x faster. It produces a
file and is rapidly becoming the default for new projects.

Commit lock files for applications; don't commit them for libraries. Library users should be able to resolve a compatible set from the library's loose constraints — a committed lock file would force them to use your exact versions.

runs.text: Hash pinning catches tampered packages: if PyPI is compromised and a package is replaced with malicious code, the hash in your lock file will no longer match and
(enabled automatically by pip-tools) will refuse to install it.

A lock file is a photograph of your working dependency tree. requirements.txt says 'I need requests, any recent version.' The lock file says 'I need requests 2.31.0 specifically, along with these 12 other packages at these exact versions, verified by their hashes.' The photo reproduces the exact same environment anywhere.

cards.title: Monorepo vs Multi-Repo for Python
cards.teaser: A monorepo keeps all related Python packages in one repository; a multi-repo gives each package its own repo. Monorepos simplify cross-package changes and testing; multi-repos simplify independent release cadences and access control.

runs.text: , multiple Python packages live under a single git repository. A typical layout is
command installs all of them in editable mode. An atomic commit can update both packages simultaneously — impossible across repos.

setup, each package has its own repository, CI pipeline, and release process. Teams own their packages independently. The cost: cross-package changes require coordinated PRs across repositories, and you must publish intermediate versions to PyPI (or a private registry) to get the latest code into dependent packages.

items.text: Monorepos shine for tightly coupled packages that are always released together — shared libraries, microservices that must stay in sync, or feature development spanning multiple components.
Multi-repos shine for independently versioned libraries with different release cadences, different teams, or fine-grained access control requirements.
provide monorepo-aware build systems for Python that run tests and builds only for packages affected by a change.

runs.text: Start with a monorepo. Splitting into multiple repos is straightforward when a package stabilizes and needs independent releases. Merging multiple repos into one is painful and disruptive. Prefer the option that's easy to undo.

Monorepo vs multi-repo is the question of whether your team shares one apartment or has separate houses. One apartment makes coordination easy and cheap — you knock on a door. Separate houses give everyone privacy and independence — but coordinating a renovation across three houses requires a lot of scheduling. Pick based on how often you need to renovate together.

runs.text: Formatting debates (two spaces vs four, trailing commas, line length) are the most costly low-value discussions in a team codebase. An automated formatter with no configuration options removes the debate entirely — the tool decides, everyone moves on.

black and ruff are autocorrect for code style. Instead of arguing about whether to put a blank line before a return statement, you just run the formatter and it decides. Every developer on the team gets the same output regardless of how they typed the code — the formatter is the style guide, and it enforces itself.
